name: Generative ai

subjectOf.text: Reward modeling learned through interaction with users carries two structural pathologies: majority views disproportionately influence the learned reward function, and the agent may engage in reward hacking.
subjectOf.abstract: but it comes with potential issues such as the prevalence of majority views disproportionately influencing the learned reward function and the risk of reward hacking.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, How AI Models are Optimized Through Web3 Governance (2024). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=4855607
scope_conditions: reward functions learned from aggregated user interaction

subjectOf.text: The Shenzhen courts illustrate a workable three step human-in-the-loop design for generative judicial AI: the judge decides first, the LLM generates the supporting reasoning, and the judge then revises that output to finalize the judgment.
subjectOf.abstract: A notable case study from Shenzhen, China, illustrates a three-step interaction pattern: judges make initial decisions, LLMs generate reasoning based on these decisions, and judges revise the output to finalize judgments.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Morgan A. Gray, The Evolving Role of Artificial Intelligence in Law (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5541658
scope_conditions: Chinese courts using LLMs to draft judicial opinions

subjectOf.text: Generative AI such as ChatGPT cannot produce justified beliefs aligned with virtue jurisprudence because it lacks the human virtues that responsive judging requires.
subjectOf.abstract: Generative AI, such as ChatGPT, cannot produce justified beliefs aligned with virtue jurisprudence, as it lacks the human virtues required for responsive judging.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Morgan A. Gray, The Evolving Role of Artificial Intelligence in Law (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5541658
scope_conditions: judging evaluated under a virtue jurisprudence standard

subjectOf.text: Generative AI in judicial settings is far from perfect: it can oversimplify complex judicial deliberations, reduce emotive and cognitive processes to statistical correlations, and introduce biases or interpretive errors.
subjectOf.abstract: However, these applications are far from perfect, as generative AI can oversimplify complex judicial deliberations, reduce emotive-cognitive processes to statistical correlations, and introduce biases or interpretive errors.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Morgan A. Gray, The Evolving Role of Artificial Intelligence in Law (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5541658
scope_conditions: judges using tools such as GPT-4 to draft rulings or analyze arguments

subjectOf.text: Generative AI unlocks 2.6 to 4.4 trillion dollars in annual value by automating 60 to 70 percent of work activities and reallocating 45 percent of working hours.
